Please add the maintainers of affected repositories to review.
Added @benjaminfair@google.com and @wltu@google.com who are owners of phosphor-host-postd
This feels like you're missing background here.  What is this hardware mechanism?  What standard is it documented in?

Nvidia uses ARM CPUs. The post codes are defined part of SBMR specification. Currently, the mechanism to obtain post codes was push model where bios would send the progress code to bmc and bmc would publish it. With this patch, BMC will poll at regular interval and fetch the progress code from bios.

My comment needs to be addressed in the document.

I still can’t tell from your reply if this mechanism is documented in the SBMR or you’re referring to an nvidia-proprietary solution. Either way, be explicit.

I was referring to nvidia-proprietary solution. 
Added this paragraph in the design document to highlight the same
```
It is essential to note that no industry-wide standard currently defines a
universal hardware-backed mechanism for boot progress or error code queues. The
actual hardware implementation — such as the use of scratch registers,
memory-mapped queues, or circular buffers—is OEM-specific. Each platform vendor
is responsible for defining the structure, semantics, and access methods for
these queues. The OpenBMC implementation is designed to be adaptable to both Arm
SBMR-compliant and OEM-defined hardware.
[The Arm Server Base Manageability Requirements (SBMR)](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/den0069/latest/)
specification provides requirements and recommendations for server
manageability, including standard interfaces and protocols (Redfish, IPMI) for
communication between the host and the BMC. However, SBMR does not define or
require a hardware-backed queue mechanism for boot progress or error code
reporting; instead, it standardizes software interfaces and protocols for
manageability, leaving the hardware mechanism for boot/event code storage and
retrieval as implementation-defined and OEM-specific.
```
Resolving the comment as the document is updated stating this is OEM specific design
I have no idea what a "Platform Management Controller" is.  Is this something specific to Nvidia?  Arm?  Something I'm just not familiar with?
It is OEM one so changed it to generic terminology.

@benjaminfair@google.com @wltu@google.com currently, the properties under `xyz.openbmc_project.State.Boot.Progress` are not updated from phosphor-host-postd. 
With this design, we probably will have to update `xyz.openbmc_project.State.Boot.Progress` as this application will be fetching the post code. Would that be acceptable ?

As I'm reading this design doc, its considerably more complex than it needs to be.  We're not changing anything about post codes in the system;  The only thing changing is that we're adding a new way to poll them because newer hardware has new ways to produce them (polling versus command).  The doc needs to be written as from that perspective.

If we're not planning on changing something, it doesn't need mentioned in this doc.  In theory we're only adding changes to phosphor-post-code-manager.
Yes, we are only adding changes to phosphor-host-postd. The latest patch addresses the comments.
Please be clear that we're defining a new OEM compile option into phosphor-host-postd (in the "impacts" section?).
Done.
This section is considerably longer than it needs to be and largely is a distraction from the background, which is that There exists interfaces for reading postcodes.
Acknowledged

please format this as a requirement list:

1. Must poll post codes from ARM-based processors
2. Must be able to recreate a consistent set of post codes for any given boot.
More?
Acknowledged
Remove.  This is background.
Acknowledged
This is a requirement and should be in your requirements section.
Acknowledged
Why two?  (ideally this would've been answered in your background).
Acknowledged

When I get to things like this, I have no idea if this is coming from the SBMR or something you've made up.  If there is a requirement from the SBMR, please add a reference.  If this is something you've made up, you need it as a requirement.

I've never heard of synchronized timestamps across "CPU firmware" and "PCIe device ROMs" being a thing.  What is the "shared clock source"?

Updated the document. 
Multiple IPs use the same clock to log the timestamp along with the code.

It isn't clear to me why we are dealing with BootProgress in phosphor-host-postd.  That's not how it is done today; phosphor-state-manager exposes this.  You've mentioned nothing in the entire design document but you're planning to do it different... somehow.

This sounds like it is going to lead to system-specific postcode to BootProgress mapping.  How are we going to organize that?

We are updating BootProgress property hosted by phosphor-state-manager. 
We just make a dbus set property call to set the Boot related properties hosted by phosphor-state-manager
I don't know what this is in reference to.  Please elaborate.
This sounds like something you need specified as a "requirement" to me?  Otherwise ... why wouldn't we still choose to use something standard that already works?
Acknowledged

I don't understand how this is an "Alternative Considered".  Isn't this your implementation?  I quote: 

> The actual hardware implementation — such as the use of scratch registers,
> memory-mapped queues, or circular buffers—is OEM-specific. Each platform vendor
> is responsible for defining the structure, semantics, and access methods for
> these queues.
Acknowledged
This does not seem like a "BMC Impact".  What is the point of these words?  I don't know what to make of these statements w.r.t. the design and/or its shortcomings and/or how it will affect the BMC.
Updated the Impacts section
"will"?
Acknowledged
But you're changing the transport mechanism and not the "infrastructure", right?
Addressed the comment
Please mark comments as resolved if you feel they are so.  There are still 7 unresolved comments on this, which means reviewers are likely to stay away.
ck

> ck

Not sure where this came from.  Please ignore.
This isn't entirely true, right?  There is also "ipmi-snoop" mode.
How is the design going to handle multi-host designs.  1 BMC monitoring N hosts.  The design should be able to have separate post-code "queues" for the distinct host slices.

Is there no possible method of an interrupt here?  Or at least a GPIO asserting something is in the queue?  Having the BMC to have to poll is no ideal, especially because post codes come in very quickly, so I assume you're going to want a quick polling interval.

What is a default / expected polling interval for this proposal?

You might consider some sort of back-off and/or non-linear polling interval.  I see, generally, two states:

1. The system just started booting and you're going to get a flurry of post codes.
2. The system is running and you're rarely going to get a new post code.

State (1) can maybe be identified by PSM dbus properties (ie. a watch on the Chassis or Host).  State (2) can be identified by a long period without post codes.

How is the BMC expected to merge boot entries if they are coming in from multiple sources?  I think you need to specify how this might be done.

If I have an empty queue and I read socket 0, I might get postcode `{ B, Bp }`.  Immediately after that I read socket 1, I might get postcode `{ A, Ap }`.  I have to have saved `{ B, Bp }` and not emitted the `Raw` update, so that I can first send `{ A, Ap }` even though I didn't know it existed at the time I got `{B, Bp }`.

How are you going to ever know when you get a post code that you've gotten all the post codes preceding it?
Do we need to change the interface to also have a timestamp now?

We need more clarity on which are "update a dbus property in this process" and which are "update a dbus property in another process".  From my reading of your other responses, it seems like `Boot.Raw` is implemented _here_ but `BootProgress` is implemented _elsewhere_.  The diagram needs clarity.

What is the timestamp representing?  clock ticks?  uSec?  How do you deal with:

1. time wrap
2. post codes with the same timestamp
We have support for post codes which are longer than this.  Please make sure your design aligns there.

I've still gotten this far into the document and not been told that this is an OEM protocol.  At least before you introduce this table you need to identify this as the Nvidia protocol (and specify which chip will support it).
nit: Can you reduce the width of this table by 1 character.  Every single line wraps with just an extra `|`.

This will not be sufficient for:

(1) duplicate timestamps
(2) timestamp wrapping

Honestly, a vector is probably better here because you at least get stable sorting.  You can insert to the back and use a stable-sort algorithm to bubble it up into the right position.

Please ensure your data structure aligns with the types used in Postcode.Raw.  We should as early as possible get from your hardware design to something reusable, so that next generation when your hardware designers realize they want 64 bit post codes we have very little code that needs to be changed.

How is this decoding going to be specified?  I don't think this belongs in phosphor-host-postd.  @amithash@meta.com just added support in phosphor-post-code-manager for something very similar (Ibaa09fb88190a344fd7c4fadd24dda4aa4ae0633) and I think it could be enhanced here.  I also gave him feedback on the ML that he has not incorporated yet: https://lore.kernel.org/openbmc/aDmv-MAXX2QFsLlp@heinlein/

The important thing to me is we should be able to specify these configs on a per-machine / per-processor basis so that the decoding is not deeply embedded in C++ code.  You're going to need to change this for every processor generation plus you often will have OEM tweaks (ie. Meta's BIOS might have slightly different, additional post codes).  We don't want to go down a path where we need N compile flags in phosphor-host-postd to get the correct behavior.

Ideally we get phosphor-host-postd to a point where this can be enabled all the time and only used when the EM config points to it.  We'd prefer to stop adding new compile-time options that are machine-specific.
